data.text/html:
Mixed models, explained by touching them

An interactive companion to Simplistics (QuantPsych): "Simple Explanation of Mixed Models (Hierarchical Linear Models, Multilevel Models)". Mixed models, hierarchical linear models (HLM), multilevel models, and mixed-effects models are the same thing. They are a tool for data that comes in clusters: clients of the same therapist, students of the same teacher, or the same person measured again and again.Route through this notebook (the video's order):
# Idea You will...
1 Duplicating your data make copies of a thesis dataset and watch p fall
2 Clustering is partial duplication run thousands of fake classroom studies in an animated simulator
3 What mixed models do geometrically drag hospitals around and break a regression line
4 The technical caveat: lines are pulled toward the fixed effect see estimates shrink toward the average
5 Fixed vs random intercepts and slopes build the four model types by dragging lines
6 Sandbox, quiz, recap experiment freely, then test yourself
Color language (used throughout): gray dashed = naive model that ignores clusters · black = the fixed effect (the average line across clusters) · colors = individual clusters (their random effects) · red = danger: a false positive or a misleading result.

data.text/markdown:
1 · The duplicate trick: why independence matters

The video opens with a story. An undergraduate honors thesis has 67 participants and a p-value just above .05. The tempting idea: "If sample size is the only thing stopping me... why not just duplicate my data?" The p-value asks "how likely is data like this, if there is no effect?" Getting the exact same 67 scores again from 67 new people has a probability of essentially zero. A copy has a probability of one. A copy adds no new information, but the formula still counts it as new evidence: ||[t = r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad n \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; t\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; p \downarrow||]Every test that uses probabilities assumes the rows are independent. Use the slider to copy the dataset.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Clustering is partial duplication

Nobody duplicates data on purpose. But if you ask a stranger about a Supreme Court decision, you cannot predict their answer from the narrator's answer. If you ask his brother (same house, same parents, same genes), the answer is almost a copy. The same thing happens with repeated measures (you now vs. you in 6 months), family members, and students taught by the same teacher. Scores that are correlated within a group are clustered. The amount of copying is the intraclass correlation, ρ (ICC): the share of the variance that is shared by everyone in a cluster. ||[y_{ij} = \mu + u_j + \varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \rho = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(u_j)}{\operatorname{Var}(u_j) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{ij})}||]A cluster of m people is worth only ||(m / \text{DE}||) independent people, where ||(\text{DE} = 1 + (m-1)\rho||) is the design effect. The simulator: each study gives a teaching intervention to half the classrooms. The intervention does nothing (the null is true). Each dot is one study's t-statistic:
  • top row (naive): treat every student as independent, which is a plain t-test on all students.
  • bottom row (cluster-aware): compare classroom means, which is a t-test on J clusters.
A red dot is a false positive. An honest test should produce red dots about 5% of the time.

data.text/markdown:
3 · What mixed models do geometrically: the hospital example

The video's second consequence of ignoring clusters is that the relationship itself can be deceiving. On the x-axis is symptom severity, and on the y-axis is the survival rate. If you fit one line through everything, the result seems to say "the more severe your symptoms, the more likely you are to survive". That seems weird. Now color the dots by hospital: In-N-Out, Cyprus, University Medical. University Medical takes only severe patients, and In-N-Out takes only mild ones. Inside each hospital, the relationship is negative.
Mixed models (roughly) fit a separate line for each cluster (the random effects), then average them into one line (the fixed effect).
||[\text{survival}_{ij} = \underbrace{\gamma_0 + \gamma_1\,\text{severity}_{ij}}_{\text{fixed effect (black)}} + \underbrace{u_{0j}}_{\text{hospital } j\text{'s own shift}} + \varepsilon_{ij}||]Drag each hospital (the big circle) to change who it treats and how well it does. The points move with it. The gray dashed line ignores clusters. The black line is the average of the colored hospital lines.

data.text/markdown:
4 · The technical caveat: cluster lines are pulled toward the fixed effect

The video adds a caveat: "We don't actually fit separate regression lines for each cluster. The cluster lines are biased toward the fixed effect." This is called partial pooling or shrinkage. Each cluster's estimate is a weighted compromise between its own data and the overall average: ||[\hat\mu_j^{\text{mixed}} = \lambda_j\,\bar y_j + (1-\lambda_j)\,\hat\gamma_0, \qquad \lambda_j = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2/n_j}||]Here, ||(\tau||) is the spread between clusters, ||(\sigma||) is the noise within clusters, and ||(n_j||) is the cluster size. Small, noisy clusters do not get much say, so they are pulled toward the average. Large clusters keep their own value. Below are 8 schools with very different numbers of students. A hollow circle is the school's raw mean (no pooling). A filled circle is the mixed-model estimate. A tick is the true value.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLook at school 1 (n = 3) versus school 8 (n = 80). The small school's arrow is long, and the large school's arrow barely moves.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eRaise σ to 40. Everything collapses toward the black line, because noisy data earns less trust.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eRaise τ to 15 and lower σ to 3. The schools really differ, so the model mostly trusts each school (λ → 1). Re-roll a few times and compare the two RMS errors.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Fixed vs. random effects: the four model shapes

  • Random: each cluster gets its own value (its own intercept and/or slope).
  • Fixed: everyone gets the same value, which is the average across clusters.
The video's examples:
  • Random intercepts, fixed slopes (very common): calories → weight gain has the same slope in every school, but each school starts at its own level. Treatment effects in therapist or school studies, and the male–female gap across schools, are other examples. Result: parallel lines.
  • Random intercepts and random slopes (probably the most common): every cluster gets its own line.
  • Fixed intercepts, random slopes (rare and weird): all lines start at the same point and fan out. "I've never seen this in practice."
||[y_{ij} = (\gamma_0 + u_{0j}) + (\gamma_1 + u_{1j})\,x_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}||]Remove ||(u_{0j}||) to make the intercept fixed, and remove ||(u_{1j}||) to make the slope fixed. Build the shapes yourself: drag a circle (at x = 0) to move the intercept of a line, and drag a square (at x = 10) to tilt the line. The black dashed line is the fixed effect (the average line).

data.text/markdown:
6 · Sandbox: generate clustered data and fit any model

Choose the true data-generating process, choose a model, and compare the estimated fixed slope (and its standard error) with the truth. The between-cluster confound shifts clusters that have high x upward or downward, as in the hospital example.
